title: PR #54871 added a user notification-option DELETE endpoint that looks up the NotificationSettingOption by id without restricting it to the URL's user, so any user can delete other users' alert notification settings.

vulnerable_findings.explanation: The delete() endpoint fetches a NotificationSettingOption by notification_option_id without verifying that it belongs to the authenticated user. The endpoint receives a user parameter from UserEndpoint, but only queries by id without checking user_id ownership. An attacker can delete any notification option by guessing or enumerating IDs.

findings.explanation: The code uses Django ORM's get() method with keyword arguments (id=notification_option_id). The id parameter is passed as a keyword argument to a Django query, which uses parameterized queries internally. Django ORM automatically parameterizes all queries, preventing SQL injection.
The code uses Django ORM's filter() method with keyword arguments (user_id=user.id). All database queries use Django ORM's parameterized query system, which prevents SQL injection.

The delete() endpoint fetches a NotificationSettingOption by notification_option_id without verifying that it belongs to the authenticated user. The endpoint receives a user parameter from UserEndpoint, but only queries by id without checking user_id ownership. An attacker can delete any notification option by guessing or enumerating IDs.

The put() endpoint uses user.id in update_or_create() queries, which appears to correctly scope operations to the authenticated user. However, the scope_identifier parameter comes from user-controlled request.data without apparent validation that the user owns/has access to that scope. If scope_identifier refers to a team or organization ID, an unauthorized user might modify settings for resources they don't own.

findings.suggested_fix: Validate that the user has permission to modify settings for the requested scope_identifier (e.g., verify team/org membership if scope_type is TEAM or ORGANIZATION)
